chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Is'haq ibn 'Ammar, who said:

I said to Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him) and asked him about the affluent woman who had performed the Hajj of Islam (her first obligatory Hajj), so she says to her husband, 'Take me to Hajj from my own wealth.' Is it for him to forbid her? He said: 'Yes. He should say, 'My right upon you is greater than your right upon me, with regard to this.'

key_terms.أَحِجِّنِي: Take me to Hajj / Accompany me to Hajj
key_terms.حَجَّةَ الْإِسْلَامِ: The first obligatory Hajj performed by a Muslim
key_terms.حَقِّي عَلَيْكِ: My right upon you (husband's right of guardianship)

ai.seo_question: Does a husband have the right to prevent his wife from performing Hajj using her own money?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Kafi, Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies that a wealthy woman's independent right to perform Hajj is subject to her husband's permission, as his right of guardianship (haqq) in this specific context supersedes hers. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle of 'nushuz' (obedience/submission) within marriage, where the husband's consent is a prerequisite for the wife's voluntary acts of worship that require her absence from the home. It highlights the balance between a woman's religious obligations and her marital duties, emphasizing that financial independence does not automatically grant autonomy in all religious matters without spousal approval.
